Industry observers note that A one-hour YouTube talk contains roughly nine thousand words, and finding the one point you need can take longer than watching the whole thing. A transcript solves that. With text in hand you can search for a phrase, quote an expert accurately, turn a webinar into a blog post, create subtitles or feed a summary tool.

According to recent reports, plenty of tools now promise instant YouTube transcripts, but they work in different ways. Some read the captions YouTube already has. Others listen to the audio themselves and produce a fresh transcript. That difference affects accuracy, speed and cost more than any feature list does. This guide compares six options, explains how each works and points out where each one falls short. Plans and limits change often, so confirm current details on each vendor's site.

Caption extraction. The tool pulls the captions attached to a video, either written by the creator or generated automatically by YouTube. It is fast and usually free, but it is only as good as those captions. YouTube notes that its automatic captions come from machine learning, so quality may vary, and accents, background noise and overlapping speakers can cause errors. Captions may also be missing entirely for some videos.

It has been revealed that fresh speech recognition. The tool takes the audio and runs its own speech-to-text model. This can be more accurate on difficult recordings and works when no captions exist, but it takes longer and often costs money.

Lynote is built for exactly this job. Paste a YouTube link, search by keyword or add a playlist, and it returns a timestamped transcript with an AI summary. Batch mode accepts up to 10 videos at once. The tool lists transcription in more than 100 languages, translation into 25, auto-chapters, one-click copy and TXT download, with SRT export also mentioned. The page says transcripts are free, with no sign-up required.

Best for: Students, researchers and marketers who want a quick, readable transcript or summary from a public video without installing anything.

Limitations: It extracts YouTube captions, so videos without captions cannot be processed. If the original captions are poor, the transcript will be too. For critical accuracy, review the text or use a service with human verification.

Before you install anything, check what YouTube already gives you. Many videos show a transcript option in the description area, and creators can review and edit automatic captions in YouTube Studio under Subtitles. YouTube offers automatic captions in dozens of languages for long-form videos and Shorts.

Best for: Quick lookups on videos that already have decent captions.

Sources indicate that limitations: Captions may not generate for videos with poor sound, long silences, overlapping speakers, mixed languages or unsupported languages. Export options are minimal, and there is no summary or cleanup.

Notta transcribes uploaded audio and video files and also accepts YouTube links. It lists support for 58 languages, real-time and bilingual transcription, and AI Notes that produce summaries and action items. A free plan includes 120 transcription minutes per month at the time of writing.

Best for: Professionals who handle a mix of recordings, meetings and YouTube videos in one place.

Limitations: The free minutes disappear rapidly if you process long videos, and the strongest features sit behind paid plans.

According to recent reports, descript is an audio and video editor built around text. It transcribes recordings automatically, and deleting a word in the transcript removes the matching footage. You can import video, audio or a Zoom recording, and there is a free tier that does not require a credit card.

Best for: Creators who want to clean up their own videos and podcasts, not just read a transcript.

Sources indicate that limitations: It is an editor first, so it is more than you need for a quick YouTube lookup. It works with files you own, so you need the source media rather than a public link.

According to recent reports, rev offers both AI and human transcription. It advertises AI transcripts at 96 percent or better accuracy in minutes, and human transcripts at 99 percent or better, guaranteed within 12 hours. AI transcription covers 37 or more languages, while human transcription is English only. Pay-as-you-go rates start at $0.25 per minute for AI, and human transcription is listed at $1.99 per minute.

Best for: Legal, research and media work where mistakes are costly and a human check is worth paying for.

Industry observers note that limitations: The cost climbs for long videos, and the human option is slower than instant AI tools. Those accuracy figures are the vendor's own claims, so test your own audio.

Whisper is OpenAI's open-source speech recognition model, released under the MIT license. It handles multilingual transcription, translation into English and language identification. You install it with pip and need ffmpeg, and it comes in several model sizes from tiny to large, so you can trade speed against accuracy and hardware demands.

Best for: Developers building their own pipeline and teams with sensitive audio they prefer to keep on their own machines.

Limitations: You supply the audio, which means downloading it yourself and respecting the video owner's rights and YouTube's terms. Larger models need a capable GPU, and there is no built-in interface for non-technical users.

Sources indicate that start with the source. If the video already has good captions, a link-based tool is the fastest route. If the audio is difficult or the stakes are high, pick a tool that runs its own recognition or offers human review. If you are processing hundreds of videos or handling private recordings, look at Whisper or a paid platform with bulk features.

According to recent reports, whatever you choose, treat the transcript as a first draft. Check names, numbers and technical terms against the video before you publish or quote anything, and credit the original creator.

According to recent reports, there is no single best transcript generator. Caption-based tools are quick and free, recognition-based tools are better when captions fall short, and human-verified services make sense when accuracy matters most. Try two or three on a video you know well, compare the results and keep a human in the loop for anything you publish.

Sources indicate that can I get a transcript if a video has no captions? Caption-extraction tools cannot. You need a tool that runs its own speech recognition on the audio, such as the options above that transcribe files.

Are AI transcripts accurate enough to publish? Often they are close, but not perfect. Accents, noise and technical terms cause mistakes, so review before publishing.

What is the difference between a transcript and subtitles? A transcript is the full text, while subtitles are timed text shown on screen. Many tools can export both, often as SRT files.

#34897. A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2319 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2319 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it?
  • In a recent development, researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself.
  • Industry observers note that the research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.

In a recent development, researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.

Industry observers note that the research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.

Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult.

Conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.

Recent findings suggest that this unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.

Sources indicate that "In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," notes Egues.

Industry observers note that to minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.

Industry observers note that the term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.

Although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.

"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," claims the researcher.

A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal.

The proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.

Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.

These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.

Sources indicate that "In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.

The key to the new approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.

The researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.

Industry observers note that crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.

"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.

How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information.

To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.

One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.

According to recent reports, the first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.

It has been revealed that according to the fresh research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.

"Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.

According to recent reports, this means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.

A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage.

Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.

Ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect.".

Sources indicate that the researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.

Sources indicate that "Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," notes Egues.

According to recent reports, this behavior is notable because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.

That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.

Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor.

The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.

Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.

Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.

In a recent development, the nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.

Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.

According to recent reports, "We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small.".

The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.

Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance.

It has been revealed that in quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.

This fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.

Recent findings suggest that the proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.

"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.

The approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.

This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.

Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy.

To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.

According to recent reports, these calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.

The results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.

According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.

The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.

However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.

Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?

Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.

The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.

What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.

In a recent development, "All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.

This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely latest materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain crucial challenges.

The research offers two potentially significant advances.

From the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.

Industry observers note that from a technological perspective, the study shows how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.

According to recent reports, if future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.

More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising new way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.

#34896. Tech Report: Prefill and Decode for Concurrent Requests - Optimizing LLM Performance

📅 16 Apr 2025 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1811 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Prefill and Decode for Concurrent Requests - Optimizing LLM Performance

📅 16 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1811 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Handling load from multiple customers in parallel is crucial for the performance of LLM applications.
  • Industry observers note that at TNG, we are self-hosting numerous Large Language Models on our cluster of 24 H100 GPUs.
  • Industry observers note that most LLMs generate text token by token, which guarantees that every new token is computed based on all preceding tokens (this model property is called auto-regressive).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Handling load from multiple customers in parallel is crucial for the performance of LLM applications. In the previous part of our series on LLM performance, we discussed queueing strategies for the prioritization of different users. In this second part, we will now focus on the concurrent processing of requests, and how it impacts relevant metrics such as latency and throughput as well as GPU resource utilization.

Industry observers note that at TNG, we are self-hosting numerous Large Language Models on our cluster of 24 H100 GPUs. It supports 50 different applications, handles over 5,000 inferences per hour, and generates more than ten million tokens every day.

Industry observers note that most LLMs generate text token by token, which guarantees that every new token is computed based on all preceding tokens (this model property is called auto-regressive). The first output token depends on all prompt tokens, but the second output token already depends on all prompt tokens plus the first output token, and so on. As a consequence, token generation cannot be parallelized at the level of an individual request.

Sources indicate that in LLMs with attention mechanisms, computing a fresh token requires calculating key, value, and query vectors for each preceding token. Fortunately, the results of some particular calculations can be re-used for subsequent tokens. This concept is known as key-value (KV) cache. For every additional output token, only one more set of key and value vectors needs to be calculated and added to the KV cache. For the very first output token, however, we start with an initially empty KV cache and need to calculate as many sets of key and value vectors as there are tokens in the input prompt. Luckily, and in contrast to any later token generation, all input tokens are known from the beginning, and we can parallelize the calculation of their respective key and value vectors. This difference motivates the distinction between the prefill (computing the first output token) and the decode phase (computing any later output token).

In the prefill phase, the calculations for all input tokens can be executed in parallel, while in the decode phase, no parallelization is possible on the level of individual requests.

Recent findings suggest that the difference between the prefill and decode phases is also reflected in two key metrics for text generation: Time to first token and time per output token. The time to first token is given by the latency of the prefill phase, while the time per output token is the latency of a single decode step. Even though the prefill phase also generates only a single token, it takes much longer than a single decode step, because all input tokens need to be processed. On the other hand, the prefill phase is much faster with respect to the number of input tokens than a decode phase for the same number of output tokens (this difference is the reason why commercial LLM APIs charge input tokens at a much lower rate than ouput tokens).

Both latencies are relevant metrics for interactive applications like a chat bot. If users have to wait for more than 5 seconds before they see a response, they might think that the application is broken and leave. Similarly, if the text generation is as slow as 1 token per second, they would not be patient enough to wait until it is finished. Typical latency targets for interactive applications are 100-300ms per output token (i.e. a token generation speed of 3-10 tokens per second, at least as fast as reading speed, which ideally allows for skimming the output text as it is being generated), and a time to first token of 3 seconds or less. Both of these latency targets can be quite challenging to achieve, depending on the model size, hardware, prompt length, and concurrent load.

In a recent development, other, non-interactive use cases might not be interested in the latencies of individual requests, but only in the total token throughput (tokens per second, summed up over all concurrent requests). This could be relevant when you want to generate translations for books, or summarize code files in a large repository.

As we will see in a later section, there generally is a trade-off between maximizing the total throughput and minimizing latencies for each individual request.

Sources indicate that because of the parallelized calculation for all input tokens, the prefill phase is very GPU compute-intensive. In contrast, the decode step for an individual output token utilizes very little computational power; here, the speed is typically limited by the GPU memory bandwidth, i.e. how quickly model weights and activations (including key and value vectors) can be loaded from and accessed within the GPU memory.

Recent findings suggest that in general, token throughput can be increased until the GPU utilization (w.r.t. computational power) is saturated. In the prefill phase, a single request with a long prompt can already achieve maximum GPU utilization. In the decode phase, the GPU utilization can be increased by batch processing of multiple requests. As a consequence, when you plot the token throughput as a function of the number of concurrent requests, you see an almost linear increase in throughput at low concurrency, because this memory-bound regime benefits from larger batch sizes. Once the GPU utilization saturates and the compute-bound regime is entered, the throughput remains invariant to an increase in concurrency.

We will now consider how exactly an inference engine handles multiple requests that arrive within a short time interval.

It has been revealed that both the prefill and decode phases can make use of batching strategies to apply the same set of operations to different requests. But what are the consequences of running prefill and decode of different requests at the same time?

The most naive form of batching is called static batching. (1) You start with an empty batch, (2) you fill the batch with as many items as are waiting and as fit into the batch, (3) you process the batch until all batched items are finished, and (4) you repeat the procedure with a latest empty batch.

All requests start their prefill phase at the same time. Since prefill is just a single, but heavily parallelized, GPU operation (think of it as a very large matrix multiplication), the prefill phases of all concurrent requests are completed at the same time. Then, all decode phases start simultaneously. Requests with fewer output tokens would finish earlier, but because of the static batching the next waiting request can only start once the longest batched request has been completed.

It has been revealed that static batching optimizes the time per output token, since the decode phase is uninterrupted. The drawback is a very inefficient resource utilization. Since a single, long prompt can already saturate the compute power during prefill, handling multiple prefills in parallel does not yield a speed-up and will certainly max out GPU utilization. In contrast, the GPU will likely be underutilized during the decode phase, since even a large number of concurrent decodes is not as compute-intensive as the prefill for a long prompt.

The biggest disadvantage, however, is the potentially long time to first token. Even if some short requests finish early, the next queuing request has to wait for the longest decode in the batch to finish before its prefill can begin. Because of this flaw of static batching, inference engines typically implement continuous batching strategies. Here, any completed request is immediately removed from the batch, and the batch space is filled with the next request in line. As a consequence, every continuous batching strategy has to deal with concurrency between prefill and decode phases.

Industry observers note that in an attempt to reduce the waiting time of requests, inference engines such as vLLM and TGI schedule the prefill phase of new requests as soon as they arrive and fit into the current batch. It is possible to run the prefill of new requests in parallel with a single decode step for each of all previous requests, but since everything is executed in the same GPU operation, its duration is dominated by the prefill, and for every request in the decode phase only a single output token can be generated in that time. Therefore, this prioritization of prefills minimizes the time to first token but interrupts the decode phase of already running requests. In a chat application, customers can experience this as pausing of the streamed token generation when other users submit long prompts.

In the following measurement you can see the effect of continuous batching with a prefill-first strategy.

In a recent development, one approach to alleviate the impact of interruptive prefills on running decodes is a chunked prefill. Instead of processing the entire prompt in a single prefill step, it can be distributed over multiple chunks. Then there can be as many concurrent decode steps during prefill as there are prefill chunks (as opposed to only a single decode step per concurrent request during the entire prefill). A chunked prefill step will still take longer than an isolated decode step, but for small chunk sizes the user now experiences only a slowing-down of token generation instead of a complete pause; this reduces the average time per output token. From the perspective of the interrupting request, a chunked prefill comes with some overhead and takes a bit longer than an isolated, contiguous prefill, so there is a small increase in the time to first token. With the chunk size we now have a tuning knob for prioritizing either the time to first token or the time per output token. Typical chunk sizes are between 512 and 8192 tokens (the vLLM default was 512 when chunked prefill was first implemented, and was later updated to higher values).

According to recent reports, the biggest advantage of this strategy is, however, that chunked prefill maximizes resource efficiency. Prefill is compute-intensive, while decode is memory-bound. By running both operations in parallel, one can increase the overall throughput without being limited by GPU resources. Of course, maximum efficiency is only achieved at a certain chunk size, which in turn depends on the exact load pattern.

Industry observers note that in a standard vLLM deployment and for evenly sized requests, we observed that chunked prefill increased the total token throughput by +50%. It is now enabled for every vLLM deployment of self-hosted LLMs at TNG. Overall, chunked prefill is a good default strategy for most use cases. Optimizing the chunk size, however, is quite difficult in environments with unpredictable load patterns (like TNG with its many diverse applications); typically, you stick with the defaults.

Regardless of the exact chunk size configuration, concurrent processing with chunked prefill comes with two challenges that we will address in the next article.

I just wonder how chunked prefill enable sprefill and decode request be processed in a single batch.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Finetuning olmOCR to be a faithful OCR-Engine

📅 22 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (851 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recently, the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence introduced olmOCR, a model that has demonstrated impressive results in converting PDFs into clean, linearized plain text while preserving structured content.
  • In this example, crucial information in the header and footer marked as red, is ignored by olmOCR.
  • In a recent development, optical Character Recognition has broad applications in various business use cases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recently, the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence introduced olmOCR, a model that has demonstrated impressive results in converting PDFs into clean, linearized plain text while preserving structured content. However, olmOCR's primary use case is to provide more training data for Large Language Models and therefore ignores extraneous information like headers and footers in documents. While this is beneficial for generating training data, it is insufficient for real business applications where crucial information often resides in the header and footer part of the text (think of invoices, for example). This article describes how we fine-tuned the original olmOCR-7B-0225-preview to be a faithful OCR engine, enabling it to support a broader range of applications.

In this example, crucial information in the header and footer marked as red, is ignored by olmOCR.

In a recent development, optical Character Recognition has broad applications in various business use cases. For a long time, the predominant paradigm for AI-based OCR engines have been pipeline-based systems. These are comprised of multiple machine-learning components, e.g., section segmentation, table parsing, character recognition, etc., chained together. However, one fundamental flaw of this approach is that the extracted results mostly do not flatten the context in a way that adheres to logical reading order, also known as linearization. This is particularly challenging for layout-rich documents with floating elements like multi-column documents with floating diagrams, headers, footers, etc. With the recent advent of Vision Language Models, a lot of effort has been put into leveraging them as alternative OCR systems to tackle this problem.

During our testing of the olmOCR model published on Hugging Face for business applications like invoice parsing, we observed a consistent omission of important information in the headers and footers. This was expected, as the dataset used to train olmOCR, olmOCR-mix-0225, intentionally excludes extraneous information in these areas to maintain a natural reading flow, as such information cannot be meaningfully predicted in the context of next-token prediction for training.

In a recent development, to address this limitation and enable comprehensive information extraction, we utilized Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct to generate a dataset of 8,000 documents that captures all relevant information, as one would expect from a reliable OCR engine. We based our training setup on the open-sourced olmOCR training pipeline, utilizing 4 gradient accumulation steps on an 8xH100 Nvidia node, for a total of 2.5 epochs. The default hyperparameters worked quite well for us, eliminating the need for resource-intensive hyperparameter search. The experiment tracking with MlLflow highlighted the following results:.

For evaluation, we utilized a customized version of the olmOCR-mix-0225 eval-datasets, which include header and footer information, also acquired with Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct.

Once the training was done, it was time to put our model to the test.

It has been revealed that we did a qualitative assessment of documents where crucial information was missing after parsing its content. Our inference setup is identical to the one by olmOCR, utilizing the special prompting strategy called document anchoring that preserves any born-digital content from each page. This technique extracts the raw tex blocks and position information to prompt VLMs alongside the rasterized image.

Recent findings suggest that we provide several examples of the original response and the response of the fine-tuned model below. We marked crucial missing information in red.

Overall, we are happy with the results, as now all information, including extraneous data, will be extracted and the model is still able to parse simple tables. Notably, we noticed that for some examples, the quality of the resulting output can change significantly with different temperatures.

Industry observers note that OCR is crucial for extracting structured information from documents. The ability of end-to-end-systems like olmOCR to linearize content gives them a strong advantage over traditional systems. With our fine-tuned version, we can now faithfully extract text including header and footer sections from various documents, which is crucial for business use cases such as invoice parsing. We are curious about how future models will evolve in this fast-paced domain. Special thanks to the Allen Institute for AI for open-sourcing their model, dataset, and code.

If you're curious to try out our finetuned olmOCR-model, we have open-sourced it on HuggingFace.

It has been revealed that we chose the 8xH100 setup primarily for speed and convenience, since we had multiple experimental runs. Our final training run lasted 6 hours, so it was definitely overkill. But we rented the cluster via a cloud platform, which was a flexible, low-commitment choice; we could easily spin up/down instances as needed. Also, in terms of GPU memory, less would be definitely sufficient, probably two GPUs are already enough.

A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1533 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles.
  • But position and time are different.
  • In a recent development, the discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.

But position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.

In a recent development, the discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.

Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds.

Understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.

Recent findings suggest that however, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.

At RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.

Recent findings suggest that tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with key changes taking place over just attoseconds.

Industry observers note that to appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.

In a recent development, making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.

Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling.

To observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a new laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.

In the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.

According to recent reports, the researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.

Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond.".

In a recent development, this approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It highlighted that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.

What makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.

This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.

"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.

A Surprising 500-Attosecond Delay.

To understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit.".

Their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.

At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become crucial simultaneously.

For example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit.".

The team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.

The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.

A Hidden Tradeoff Between Space and Time.

Sources indicate that raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially.".

According to recent reports, in other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.

To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.

This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.

Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.

It has been revealed that the findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.

Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?

Beyond revealing a new aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.

One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.

It has been revealed that transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.

Such extreme conditions could give scientists new ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.

In a recent development, "In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.

The implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.

"In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the currently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.

That possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a latest foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.

Sources indicate that for Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.

You've finished building your website. The HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files are ready, everything works locally, and now you need somewhere to publish it.

Sources indicate that static website hosting is one of the simplest ways to get a website online. Many providers offer free plans, and you don't need to maintain a traditional web server.

Industry observers note that the harder part is choosing the right provider. Some let you upload a single HTML file and share it immediately. Others connect to GitHub, automatically deploy code changes, and support entire development teams.

We've compared eight static hosting providers, including TiinyHost, Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, Vercel, and GitHub Pages. Below, you'll find their free hosting limits, pricing, advantages, and drawbacks, along with recommendations for different types of projects.

Static website hosting is a service that stores and delivers pre-built website files, including HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, and fonts.

It has been revealed that unlike traditional server-rendered websites, static sites don't need a server to generate each page when someone visits. The HTML is already prepared and can be delivered directly to the visitor's browser.

It has been revealed that that doesn't mean static websites can't be interactive. JavaScript can still handle navigation, forms, filtering, and other features. Static sites can also communicate with external APIs or databases.

The main distinction is how pages are generated.

You can write a static website using plain HTML or generate one with frameworks and tools such as Astro, Hugo, Eleventy, or Next.js static export.

Static hosting is also commonly associated with Jamstack, an approach that separates the front end from back-end services.

There are three practical reasons:.

Lower hosting costs: Many providers let you publish smaller websites for free.

Simpler maintenance: There's no application server or server-side runtime to maintain for the static pages themselves.

Efficient content delivery: Static files can be cached across a content delivery network (CDN), reducing the distance between visitors and website assets.

There are limitations, too. If your website requires user authentication, database operations, or server-side functionality, you'll need additional services or a hosting platform that supports them.

We compared eight providers based on their deployment methods, free strategy allowances, pricing, and suitability for different projects.

Free hosting limits: Bandwidth, storage, build allowances, and restrictions.

Deployment process: Whether you can upload files directly or need a Git repository.

Custom domains and HTTPS: Support for publishing under your own domain.

Development features: Automatic deployments, preview environments, and integrations.

Pricing: What happens when a project exceeds its free allowance.

Usage restrictions: Whether free hosting is suitable for commercial projects.

The following table summarizes the main differences between all eight services.

It has been revealed that free plans aren't directly comparable. For example, Vercel restricts its Hobby plan to personal, non-commercial use, while GitHub Pages prohibits using the service as free hosting for an online business or commercial SaaS.

Recent findings suggest that bandwidth limits also aren't the same as visitor limits. A website serving large images or downloadable files can consume its monthly allowance with relatively few visitors.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, we are excited to open-source PipelineRL, an experimental RL implementation that tackles a fundamental challenge in large-scale Reinforcement Learning with LLMs: the trade-off between inference throughput and on-policy data collection.
  • In this blog post, we show that 1) inflight weight updates do not harm the training process and 2) PipelineRL achieves competitive results compared to Open-Reasoner-Zero, while using a simpler RL algorithm.
  • In conventional RL approaches (Figure 1a), there is a trade-off between high throughput inference and on-policy data collection.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we are excited to open-source PipelineRL, an experimental RL implementation that tackles a fundamental challenge in large-scale Reinforcement Learning with LLMs: the trade-off between inference throughput and on-policy data collection. PipelineRL's key innovation is inflight weight updates during RL training (see Figure 1 below). This allows PipelineRL to achieve constantly high inference throughput and minimize the lag between the weights used for rollouts and the most recently updated model weights. The result: fast and stable RL training for large language models.

In this blog post, we show that 1) inflight weight updates do not harm the training process and 2) PipelineRL achieves competitive results compared to Open-Reasoner-Zero, while using a simpler RL algorithm. We also present the modular PipelineRL architecture that facilitates trying latest inference / trainer combinations.

In conventional RL approaches (Figure 1a), there is a trade-off between high throughput inference and on-policy data collection. To explain this trade-off let us first define conventional RL algorithmically:.

Industry observers note that to achieve high throughput, the inference servers must use large batch sizes and, therefore, generate data for multiple policy optimization steps. However, each optimization step increases the lag between the current policy and the data collected using the inference policy, progressively making collected data more off-policy and less effective for training. On-policy learning requires data for a single optimization step. But producing small amounts of data with many GPUs is inefficient because this means the per-GPU batch size is small. Furthermore the batch size goes down as the inference server finishes the short sequences and has only the few longest sequences in progress.

It has been revealed that pipelineRL (Figure 1b) remediates this trade-off through inflight weight updates. We update the weights in inference servers after each optimizer step without ever stopping inference. We only pause the inference at all inference servers for just the time needed to receive the new weights. Inflight weight updates allow the inference server to constantly maintain the optimal batch size while simultaneously ensuring data remains on-policy or near on-policy, which leads to better GPU utilization and more effective learning, respectively.

To demonstrate the effectiveness of PipelineRL and the benefits of inflight weight updates, we trained a 7B model and 32B model on the Open-Reasoner-Zero dataset. Looking at the learning curves we see that PipelineRL matches or exceeds the performance of Open-Reasoner on the popular reasoning test benchmarks: AIME 2024 and MATH 500 (see Figure 2 above).

Notably, our RL implementation is much simpler than Open-Reasoner-Zero. While Open-Reasoner-Zero uses a value function, our implementation is a simplified version of GRPO. In particular, we found that the trust region importance weight clamping is not needed for stable training. Neither was overlong sequence filtering or reward shaping from the DAPO paper. For normalizing the loss we just use the number of sequences in the batch as the denominator, giving equal weights to all tokens. We used no KL penalty and no entropy bonus (though our implementation does support reference model KL). Despite the simplicity of our implementation, or perhaps thanks to it, training is very stable as you can see in this wandb report.

One might expect that inflight weight updates would result in an unstable training process, since sequence generation proceeds with stale keys and values in the KV cache that was computed with a previous model version. However, our experiments indicate this does not adversely affect stability.

According to recent reports, pipelineRL is built to be modular and take advantage of rapid improvements in highly-specialized inference and training software (SGLang, vLLM, Nvidia Dynamo, DeepSpeed, FSDP, TorchTitan, FastLLM, etc.). We propose clear contracts between the inference and training components, allowing easy integration of fresh inference and training solutions as they become available.

The inference software must expose the following APIs to PipelineRL[1]:.

If init_process_group and request_weight_update APIs become the industry standard, one will be able to plug-and-play try using difference inference implementations with PipelineRL.

Industry observers note that pipelineRL training code feeds freshly-generated training data to trainer workers as soon as the right number of training tokens has accumulated for each of them. One can make any training software that exposes these Python APIs work with PipelineRL:.

Industry observers note that pipelineRL at the moment uses the HuggingFace accelerate library to give the user a choice between DeepSpeed and FSDP. But we found that accelerate contract is too flexible and can be confusing. We will be moving to the stricter contract as described above that will make using other trainers easier.

Industry observers note that upcoming features. Our implementation is still experimental and lacks some important functionality. Top priorities for us include using coroutines for more precise inference batch size control, multi-modal support and sequence parallel training. We would also welcome contributions of more inference server and trainer integrations. We will not, however, try to make the pipeline-rl repo a framework that supports all possible algorithms and reward functions. Our take is that pipeline-rl should be a hackable and fast reference implementation of GRPO with easily verifiable rewards. If you'd like to do a research project using PipelineRL, you can just fork the repo and have fun hacking the code!

More research coming soon. More analysis is needed to understand how inflight weight updates affect the training dynamics, and to carefully measure the speed-ups that PipelineRL brings. Also, much can be said about the similarities between PipelineRL and highly relevant prior work on asynchronous Reinforcement Learning for LLMs. For all this and more please stay tuned for our upcoming research paper!

According to recent reports, alexandre Piché wrote the first synchronous version of our RL code while working on TapeAgents. Dzmitry Bahdanau refactored the code to be asynchronous and distributed, and implemented inflight weight updates. Rafael Pardinas implemented sequence packing. Ehsan Kamaloo helped with running the experiments. Xiaoyin Chen helped with debugging the framework.

According to recent reports, we acknowledge the prior RL for LLM implementations such as TRL, OpenRLHF and veRL for the many tricks we borrowed from them. Artifacts from other open-source reasoning projects, such as Simple-RL, Deepscaler, DAPO and OpenReasoner were instrumental for stabilizing PipelineRL. We would like to recognize Christopher Manning, Michael Noukhovitch for their thoughtful comments. Finally, we thank the broader ServiceNow Research team and ServiceNow CoreLLM teams for being amazing colleagues.

Industry News: Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1149 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection.
  • In a recent development, unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing.
  • Industry observers note that by harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.

In a recent development, unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a latest form of computer memory.

Industry observers note that by harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," says Yiwen Chu.

Sources indicate that the breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.

Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers.

The researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an key role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.

Industry observers note that chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.

The major difference lies in how that information is stored.

"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.

According to recent reports, quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are currently beyond their practical capabilities.

Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better.

According to recent reports, one of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.

In the newly introduced system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.

Many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.

Industry observers note that however, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.

In a recent development, mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.

Sources indicate that another key benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.

Newly introduced Quantum Computer Passes Major Tests.

The research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.

Recent findings suggest that the achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.

Recent findings suggest that to evaluate the system, the researchers tested two vital computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.

"The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.

Successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments showed that the new architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.

A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers.

Industry observers note that one of the most significant findings is that the newly introduced system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.

Recent findings suggest that however, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.

Chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.

Sources indicate that practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising latest route toward making those machines a reality.

Introducing AutoRound: Intel’s Advanced Quantization for LLMs and VLMs

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) continue to grow in size and complexity, deploying them efficiently becomes increasingly challenging.
  • AutoRound is a weight-only post-training quantization (PTQ) method developed by Intel.
  • Despite its strong performance, AutoRound is fast and lightweight — quantizing a 72B model takes just 37 minutes on an A100 GPU under light mode.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) continue to grow in size and complexity, deploying them efficiently becomes increasingly challenging. Quantization offers a solution by reducing model size and inference latency. Intel's AutoRound emerges as a cutting-edge quantization tool that balances accuracy, efficiency, and compatibility.

AutoRound is a weight-only post-training quantization (PTQ) method developed by Intel. It uses signed gradient descent to jointly optimize weight rounding and clipping ranges, enabling accurate low-bit quantization (e.g., INT2 - INT8) with minimal accuracy loss in most scenarios. For example, at INT2, it outperforms popular baselines by up to 2.1x higher in relative accuracy. The image below provides an overview of the core algorithm in AutoRound. For more details, please refer to our paper.

Despite its strong performance, AutoRound is fast and lightweight — quantizing a 72B model takes just 37 minutes on an A100 GPU under light mode. It also supports mixed-bit tuning, lm-head quantization, GPTQ/AWQ/GGUF format exporting, and flexible tuning recipes.

AutoRound delivers highly promising results, particularly in low-bit quantization scenarios. Evaluations across a variety of tasks show that it outperforms popular methods by a wide margin at 2-bit precision (source). At 4 bits, AutoRound continues to hold a competitive edge in most cases, as demonstrated on the Low-Bit Open LLM Leaderboard.

In a recent development, LLMs: AutoRound supports nearly all popular LLM architectures, including well-known models like Qwen, LLaMA, and DeepSeek. Ready-to-use quantized models are available on Hugging Face through collections such as OPEA, Kaitchup, and fbaldassarri.

Recent findings suggest that VLMs: AutoRound supports over 10 vision-language models (VLMs), including Mistral-Small-3.1, Gemma3, and more. You can find the full list in the README, and ready-to-use quantized models are available in the OPEA Hugging Face collection. For models not yet supported, you can still apply our RTN method with --iters 0. No tuning is required, but some accuracy loss is expected.

Sources indicate that autoRound requires only 200 tuning steps and a small calibration dataset (as few as 128 samples) to achieve high accuracy. This efficiency translates to faster quantization times and reduced resource consumption compared to other int2 methods, which are more computationally intensive.

Currently, only offline mode is supported to generate quantized models.

AutoRound also offers another two recipes, auto-round-best and auto-round-light, designed for optimal accuracy and improved speed, respectively.

Industry observers note that for 2 bits, we recommend using auto-round-best or auto-round. For a comparison of the three recipes, please refer to the table below.

W4G128 Average Accuracy of 13 tasks (mmlu-pro, if_eval, gsm8k, etc) and Time Cost Results (Testing was conducted on the Nvidia A100 80G using the version of PyTorch 2.6.0 with enable_torch_compile):.

This setting offers a better trade-off between accuracy and tuning cost, and is recommended in all scenarios.

For the best/light settings of AutoRound for API usage or mixed-bit configurations, please refer to AutoRound README.

AutoRound automatically selects the best available backend based on the installed libraries and prompts the user to install additional libraries when a better backend is found. For more details, please refer to HF README or AutoRound README.

Industry observers note that most GPTQ/AWQ models can be converted to the AutoRound format for better compatibility and support with Intel devices. Please note that the quantization config will be changed if the model is serialized.

It has been revealed that autoRound offers a meaningful improvement step forward in post-training quantization for large language and vision-language models. By combining high accuracy, exceptional efficiency, and broad compatibility with popular models, devices, and export formats, AutoRound makes low-bit quantization both practical and powerful. Whether you're deploying LLMs at scale or experimenting with edge inference on VLMs, AutoRound provides the tools and flexibility you need to achieve optimal performance with minimal overhead. We invite you to try it out and join the growing community pushing the boundaries of efficient AI deployment.

Contributions to AutoRound are welcome and greatly appreciated! Whether it's fixing bugs, improving documentation, adding fresh features, or suggesting improvements, your help is always valued.

If you encounter any issues with auto-round, please open an problem on the AutoRound repository.

We would like to thank the open-source low-precision libraries including AutoGPTQ, AutoAWQ, GPTQModel, Triton, Marlin and ExLLaMAV2, whose CUDA kernels are used in AutoRound.

Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution
