📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that TL; DR Liger supercharges TRL’s Group Relative Policy Optimization GRPO Trainer by slashing memory usage by 40% with zero drop in model quality.
  • Fine-tuning language models using reinforcement learning (RL) is a crucial step in a model's training lifecycle for steering models towards desirable behaviours which are more complex than can be achieved through typical supervised fine-tuning.
  • However, RLHF with PPO is a very resource-hungry approach - PPO requires loading multiple models in memory (policy, value, reward, and reference models), and also requires several iterations of fine-tuning reward and base models to achieve the desired results.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that TL; DR Liger supercharges TRL’s Group Relative Policy Optimization GRPO Trainer by slashing memory usage by 40% with zero drop in model quality. We also added support for FSDP and PEFT, making it easier than ever to scale GRPO across multiple GPUs.

Fine-tuning language models using reinforcement learning (RL) is a crucial step in a model's training lifecycle for steering models towards desirable behaviours which are more complex than can be achieved through typical supervised fine-tuning. RL has traditionally been applied to optimize large language models (LLMs) using the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm. This approach, often associated with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), utilizes a separately trained reward model to guide the fine-tuning of the primary model.

However, RLHF with PPO is a very resource-hungry approach - PPO requires loading multiple models in memory (policy, value, reward, and reference models), and also requires several iterations of fine-tuning reward and base models to achieve the desired results. The success of RLHF also depends on the capability of the reward model to effectively discriminate between desired and un-desired behaviour from our model.

Industry observers note that group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has seen significant recent popularity alongside DeepSeek's R1 model. GRPO eschews the pre-trained reward model and value models used in RLHF and instead relies on verifiable reward functions which can check the correctness of a model's output in a closed-form manner without needing an external reward model. This has resulted in massive improvements when using GRPO instead of PPO for fine-tuning on domains which are easily verifiable, such as teaching a model to reason, and perform well on math and coding tasks.

The following diagram shows the GRPO vs PPO training pipeline (ref: Figure 4 of DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models):.

Industry observers note that that said, RL training still eats up a ton of GPU memory, so there's still plenty of room for optimizations here. In this blog post, we talk about an optimization that we recently added to TRL that cuts peak memory usage by 40% during GRPO Training, and we also dive into how to scale GRPO to multiple GPUs and nodes without losing performance or correctness.

We extended the Liger Chunked Loss approach to the GRPO Loss, which lets us avoid having to store the full logits in memory for every training step. The calculation of logits, which involves the model's output head, is a significant contributor to peak memory usage, especially when dealing with large vocabularies, long sequence lengths, or large batch sizes. We address this by chunking the input to the lm_head across the batch and running the forward pass one chunk at a time.

But if you just implement it in a straightforward way, you won't actually be able to reduce the peak memory since you'd still need to keep all the logits in GPU memory for the backward pass. To get around that, we calculate the gradients for each loss chunk (with respect to the input chunk and the lm_head weight) during the forward pass, and then accumulate them as we go through each chunk.

Here's the visualization of the optimization (ref: Byron Hsu):.

We recently integrated Liger GRPO with TRL in PR #3184, so now you can use the Liger GRPO loss just by setting use_liger_loss to True in your GRPOConfig and enjoy the memory savings!

Heads up: these features aren't in the latest TRL release yet, so you'll need to install TRL from source for now:.

and then you can use it like this:.

It has been revealed that we ran a bunch of GRPO experiments with and without the Liger GRPO Loss to see how things compare. For the policy model, we used Qwen3-0.6B and played around with different batch sizes. All the experiments were run on the gsm8k dataset using its reward functions.

Sources indicate that here's the plots of peak memory usage vs batch size for both FP32 and BF16 training. As expected, the memory savings get better with larger batch sizes since we chunk along the batch dimension. So when the batch size goes up, the Liger chunked loss ends up using a lot less memory, up to 40% less, compared to the regular (non-liger) version.

It has been revealed that quick note: Right now, we only support FP32, but we're working on open-sourcing BF16 support for Liger GRPO in TRL. The BF16 results shown here are from internal patches we've been testing.

Industry observers note that we also show that Liger Loss is effectively accurate. As seen in the plot, rewards over training steps stay pretty much the same as what you'd see using the standard TRL implementation.

It has been revealed that we also added FSDP and PEFT support to Liger GRPO Loss in PR #3260 and PR #3355, respectively, allowing people to easily scale their experiments across multiple GPUs or nodes. PEFT techniques such as LoRA and QLoRA reduce the number of trainable parameters by only tuning the weights of smaller adapter weights on top of the original model, significantly lowering memory pressure as gradients, activations, and optimizer states for the entire model don't need to be held in memory. Additionally, using PEFT in GRPO allows one to forgo loading a separate reference model during training, as we can obtain the original, unmodified model during training by simply disabling the LoRA adapters.

Here, we show a multi-GPU GRPO training plot using FSDP and PEFT, where we compare the maximum training batch size possible with and without the Liger Loss across different Qwen3 model sizes. We found that with Liger, we were able to bump up the batch size by around 1.5 to 1.8x!

Sources indicate that to accelerate text generation during training, Liger Loss can be effectively combined with TRL's integrated vLLM server. This significantly speeds up the collection of rollout data with minimal overhead and offers a seamless integration experience.

Note: We assign CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 to run the vLLM server on a specific GPU (GPU 1 in this case), leaving other GPUs free for training.

Configure and Run Your Training Script: Next, modify your training script to use the vLLM server. The key change is setting use_vllm=True in your GRPOConfig.

Recent findings suggest that launch the Training: Finally, run your training script using accelerate launch (or python if not using Accelerate for multi-GPU/distributed training). Make sure to target a different GPU for training if your vLLM server is occupying one.

(Assuming your script is named train.py and you want to run training on GPU 0).

By following these steps, you can leverage vLLM for faster generation turnarounds during your GRPO training with Liger Loss.

It has been revealed that with the integration of Liger-GRPO into TRL, alongside FSDP and PEFT support, fine-tuning language models with GRPO is now more memory-efficient and scalable than ever. We encourage the community to try out these newly introduced features and share their feedback to help us further improve RL training for LLMs.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that today we're sharing research that bridges two powerful paradigms in AI agent design: the expressiveness of code-based actions and the reliability of structured generation.
  • Industry observers note that figure 1: Accuracy comparison of three approaches: Structured CodeAgent (blue), CodeAgent (orange), and ToolCallingAgent (gray) on SmolBench (GAIA, MATH, SimpleQA, and Frames).
  • Sources indicate that AI agents need to take actions in the world - whether that's calling APIs, processing data, or reasoning through complex problems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that today we're sharing research that bridges two powerful paradigms in AI agent design: the expressiveness of code-based actions and the reliability of structured generation. Our findings show that forcing CodeAgents to generate both thoughts and code in a structured JSON format can significantly outperform traditional approaches across multiple benchmarks.

Industry observers note that figure 1: Accuracy comparison of three approaches: Structured CodeAgent (blue), CodeAgent (orange), and ToolCallingAgent (gray) on SmolBench (GAIA, MATH, SimpleQA, and Frames). Error bars represent 95% Confidence Intervals.

Sources indicate that AI agents need to take actions in the world - whether that's calling APIs, processing data, or reasoning through complex problems. How agents express these actions has evolved through several paradigms:.

Traditional JSON Agent: Agents generate structured JSON to call tools.

These agents operate by selecting from a list of predefined tools and generating JSON-formatted calls. This method for calling tools has been popularized by OpenAI's function calling API, and has since then been the most widely used method to call tools.

It is reliable, but limited by:.

Code Agents: Agents make use of their innate coding ability and write executable Python code directly.

This shift, first presented as CodeAct in the paper “Executable Code Actions Elicit Better LLM Agents” gave AI agents the flexibility to write arbitrary executable Python code in addition to tool-calling.

In a recent development, the key insight here is that tools are called directly from within the code, making variables and state management much more reliable. Agents can call tools within loops, functions, and conditional statements - essentially generating a dynamic graph of tool execution in each action!

However, parsing code from markdown can be error-prone which leads us to a proposition: why not use structured generation to generate code actions?

With Structured outputs, you can force the LLM to generate explicit thoughts and code as a JSON blob:.

The key difference is that the generation is enforced: basically, now instead of just being prompted to output thoughts, then code, the usage of structured outputs forces it to respect the structure.

This approach adds the reliability of structured generation to the flexibility of code execution, thus getting the best of both worlds.

Sources indicate that we compared these three paradigms across multiple benchmarks including GAIA, MATH, SimpleQA, and Frames. The results show a clear pattern: Code actions + structured generation consistently improves performance for capable models.

Across most capable models, the structured approach consistently outperformed the regular CodeAgent approach by 2-7 percentage points on average.

Our implementation of CodeAgent in smolagents extracts Python code from the LLM output, which can fail when:.

Structured generation eliminates these complications with reliable JSON parsing.

To understand why structured generation matters, we analyzed 15,724 agent traces across our benchmarks. The results are striking:.

Agent traces without parsing errors succeed 21.3% more often than those with parsing errors.

Industry observers note that this isn't just about convenience - parsing errors create a cascade of failures that significantly impact overall agent performance. When an agent can't execute its first action due to malformed code, it often struggles to recover, leading to suboptimal problem-solving paths.

Figure 2: Parsing errors in the first step reduce success rates of the agent by 21.3% and increase average steps taken from 3.18 to 4.63.

Additionally: Enforced Reasoning Process.

The use of structured generation and explicit thoughts not just prompts, but forces agents to articulate their reasoning before acting. This leads to:.

Recent findings suggest that our results also reveal a clear capability threshold: models need sufficient instruction-following ability and JSON coverage in their pre-training data to benefit from structured generation. This suggests that structured approaches work best with:.

Here's what happens when a smaller model (e.g mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3) tries to generate structured code - the cognitive load becomes too much:.

The model generates syntactically broken Python code: web_search(query="Eiffel Tower height")", - notice the malformed string with an extra quote and comma. This leads to an immediate SyntaxError and execution failure.

Industry observers note that this illustrates the "structure tax": smaller models struggle to simultaneously handle JSON formatting, Python syntax, and the actual problem-solving logic. The cognitive overhead of structured generation can overwhelm models that would otherwise perform reasonably well with simpler markdown-based code generation.

The LLM will generate something like this:.

Recent findings suggest that this research suggests we're moving toward a more nuanced understanding of agent architectures. It's not just about "what can the agent do?" but "how should the agent think about what it's doing?".

In a recent development, maybe making the reasoning process more explicit helps the model stay on track. Or maybe it's just easier to parse. Either way, it’s a win.

Industry observers note that but this is just the beginning. There are so many questions left to explore:.

For now, if you're using smolagents (or building your own CodeAgent system), consider giving structured output a try. Your parsing errors will thank you, and you might just see a nice increase in performance!

Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

No GPU left behind: Unlocking Efficiency with Co-located vLLM in TRL

📅 03 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2743 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, TRL supports training LLMs using GRPO, an online learning algorithm recently introduced in the DeepSeekMath paper.
  • This makes generation a critical step in the training loop — and also a major bottleneck.
  • According to recent reports, before TRL v0.18.0, vLLM was only supported in server mode, running as a separate process on different GPUs from the training job.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, TRL supports training LLMs using GRPO, an online learning algorithm recently introduced in the DeepSeekMath paper. In GRPO, the model learns from its own outputs: it generates responses during training, receives feedback, and uses that feedback to improve itself over time.

This makes generation a critical step in the training loop — and also a major bottleneck. To speed up generation, TRL integrates with vLLM. This combination lets you train powerful models more efficiently in GRPO setup. However, there’s a catch.

According to recent reports, before TRL v0.18.0, vLLM was only supported in server mode, running as a separate process on different GPUs from the training job. It communicated with the training script over HTTP, which made the setup modular and easy to use — but also introduced GPU inefficiencies.

This “ping-pong” between training and generation causes:.

In online learning methods like GRPO — where generation happens constantly — this inefficiency becomes even more painful. You spend more on hardware, but don't get the performance you'd expect.

So, the key question becomes: Can we share the same GPUs for both training and generation, instead of separating them?

In a recent development, the main problem was that training and inference ran on separate GPUs, leading to idle time and underutilization. The natural solution? Run both on the same GPUs. Instead of having vLLM operate as a standalone server in its own process and devices, what if vLLM could run alongside the training code, within the same distributed process group? This would let us launch a single distributed job where training and inference share the same devices, switching between tasks efficiently without wasting resources.

This approach is what we refer to as colocation. Training and inference are co-located on the same GPUs and coordinated via the same process group, allowing them to take turns smoothly — no extra hardware needed.

Previously, this wasn’t possible in TRL, which relied on vLLM as an external HTTP server. That changed with our PR #3394, which added support for vLLM’s external launcher and true integration into the training process.

Unified Execution: By embedding vLLM in the same process group, both training and inference tasks can share the same GPUs, taking turns instead of waiting on each other. This reduces idle time and boosts overall efficiency.

Skip HTTP Communication: No need for REST API calls or networking — vLLM runs inline with the training loop, avoiding overhead and latency.

Torchrun Compatibility: Works seamlessly with torchrun, so it's easy to scale across nodes with minimal config changes.

TP and DP Support: Compatible with Tensor Parallelism and Data Parallelism, making it suitable for large-scale training runs.

SPMD Execution Pattern: Uses a Single Program, Multiple Data (SPMD) model, where each GPU runs its own instance of the engine in sync. Ideal for distributed multi-GPU, multi-node setups.

Simplified Deployment: You no longer need to maintain a separate server script — vLLM is debuted and controlled directly inside your training job.

Enhanced Throughput: By avoiding idle GPUs and eliminating inter-process communication, the system delivers faster training and generation, especially important in online learning setups like GRPO.

Robust Inter-process Communication: This is more robust because it avoids the complexity of setting up distributed process groups between independent processes, as required in server mode.

Thanks to this feature, co-located training and inference is no longer a hack — it’s now first-class, scalable, and production-ready.

In a recent development, the shift from server TRL to co-located TRL is all about smarter GPU usage. The diagram below shows the difference:.

In the server TRL setup, training and inference run on separate GPUs. For example:.

In a recent development, during training steps, GPU 3 sits idle. During generation steps (inference), GPUs 0–2 are idle while GPU 3 generates outputs.

It has been revealed that in contrast, the co-located TRL setup runs both training and vLLM on the same GPUs. Each GPU:.

Training and inference take turns using the GPU’s resources — no need for dedicated devices or separate processes.

Instead of launching vLLM as a server, the trainer now launches vLLM in-process using the external launcher, as shown below:.

Co-located vLLM respects the torch.distributed process group and rank structure. This allows vLLM to be initialized alongside training without conflict and makes TP/DP setups work seamlessly:.

Co-located vLLM no longer relies on REST APIs — it runs directly in memory and communicates via native Python calls:.

To use this setup, simply set vllm_mode="colocate" in your GRPO configuration:.

Note: Depending on the model size and the overall GPU memory requirements for training, you may need to adjust the vllm_gpu_memory_utilization parameter in GRPOConfig to avoid underutilization or out-of-memory errors.

To measure the impact of colocation, we ran a series of experiments comparing the traditional server mode (where vLLM runs on a separate GPU as a standalone server) with the upcoming co-locate mode (where training and inference share the same GPUs).

In server mode, only 7 GPUs are used for training because 1 GPU is fully dedicated to the vLLM inference server.

In co-locate mode, all 8 GPUs are used for training — increasing the effective batch size by default.

Industry observers note that to ensure a fair comparison, we normalized throughput in server mode by a factor of 8/7. This adjustment accounts for the greater training capacity in co-locate mode and allows us to compare the two setups under equal training conditions.

In a recent development, when training large models like Qwen2.5-Math-72B, it's notable to use the right strategies to make training efficient, scalable, and stable across many GPUs and nodes. In our setup, we combined co-located vLLM with several key optimizations to make this work efficiently.

It has been revealed that when using co-located training, managing GPU memory is crucial so that both training and inference can run smoothly on the same devices. To support this, we added vLLM’s sleep() API into the GRPO training loop.

In a recent development, the sleep() function temporarily pauses the vLLM engine and frees up GPU memory. It supports two levels:.

Level 1: Unloads model weights from GPU (keeps them in CPU memory) and clears the KV cache. Useful when the same model will be reused soon.

It has been revealed that level 2: Unloads both model weights and KV cache entirely. Best for scenarios where the model will change or won’t be reused right away.

In GRPO, the model is updated after every step — so we use Level 2 sleep.

This small addition makes a substantial difference in enabling smooth and scalable co-located training.

To train large models like Qwen2.5-72B, we rely on DeepSpeed ZeRO Stage 3, the same setup used in plain TRL.

ZeRO helps scale large models by distributing memory across GPUs. Stage 3 goes further by partitioning:.

It has been revealed that this is essential for models that can’t fit on a single GPU. With ZeRO Stage 3, each GPU handles only a portion of the model.

"offload_optimizer": {"device": "cpu"} Moves optimizer states to CPU to free GPU memory — critical in co-located setups.

"overlap_comm": true Enables communication overlap with computation, speeding up training.

"contiguous_gradients": true Allocates gradients in a single memory block, improving memory access and reducing fragmentation.

These optimizations help train 72B models efficiently, and ensure colocation remains stable under tight memory constraints.

Industry observers note that as recommended in TRL, we use Accelerate, a lightweight library that simplifies distributed training. It handles:.

This makes the setup clean, scalable, and easy to maintain.

Even with 4 fewer GPUs, the co-locate setup is ~1.26× faster than plain TRL. This highlights the effectiveness of smarter GPU sharing and memory cleanup using sleep().

Training reward plots for co-locate and plain setups are nearly identical, demonstrating that:.

According to recent reports, we evaluated three models: Base model, Co-locate-trained model, Plain-trained model on the Math500 benchmark. Both trained models outperform the base, and the co-locate model performs on par with the plain-trained model — confirming that colocation does not compromise downstream performance.

Through our work on scaling GRPO training with co-located vLLM, we've faced several critical challenges and learned crucial lessons about efficiency, flexibility, and system design when training large models.

Tensor Parallelism Bug in vLLM ≥ 0.8.0. Tensor Parallelism (TP) with external_launcher stopped working in vLLM version 0.8.0 and above. This was tracked under Concern #15895. To identify the breaking point, we followed the approach described in this vLLM developer blog post, which provides wheels for every commit. After bisecting, we identified the breaking commit as cc10281. The root cause was determinism — the newer versions required explicitly setting the random seed. Once the seed was set, the issue went away.

Level 2 Sleep Buffer Bug. Initially, level 2 sleep didn’t work correctly when we tried to reload weights using load_weights. This concern was tracked in Issue #16564. The problem was that model buffers (like running mean/var in BatchNorm) weren’t restored after waking up from sleep. The fix came with PR #16889, which added logic to explicitly restore buffers when waking up from level 2 sleep. We now keep a copy of the original buffers and manually reapply them after loading upcoming weights.

Sources indicate that segmentation Fault on Exit. There’s still an open issue with vLLM sleep causing a segmentation fault at the end of training when closing processes. This was reported in Issue #16993. This crash happens during shutdown but does not break training itself, so we were able to complete all demos and experiments shared in this blog. However, we’re waiting for an official fix before integrating sleep() fully into TRL upstream.

These challenges were not blockers, but they required careful debugging, version control, and a deeper understanding of how vLLM manages memory and parallelism under the hood.

Co-located inference dramatically improves GPU utilization. By allowing training and generation to share the same GPUs, we eliminate idle time and reduce hardware requirements — achieving higher throughput even with fewer GPUs.

vLLM's sleep() feature is essential for large-scale colocation. It enables fine-grained control over memory usage, allowing training to fully reclaim GPU memory between generation steps — a key enabler for models like Qwen2.5-72B.

Industry observers note that deepSpeed ZeRO Stage 3 is essential for training large models. It allows extremely large networks to fit into memory by distributing model weights, gradients, and optimizer states across multiple GPUs. In our experience, enabling contiguous_gradients helped reduce memory fragmentation, while offloading the optimizer to the CPU freed up critical GPU memory — both of which were especially helpful in colocated setups.

Industry observers note that colocation is powerful but comes with trade-offs. It works best when GPU memory is carefully managed, often requiring manual tuning of memory usage parameters like vllm_gpu_memory_utilization. While it offers clear throughput benefits and reduces idle GPU time, colocation may not be ideal for models with tight memory budgets or when memory fragmentation is not well controlled. When done right, though, it unlocks significant efficiency gains.

Industry observers note that TP/DP compatibility, Accelerate, and torchrun support make deployment seamless. Despite the complexity of the underlying architecture, the entire system can be launched and scaled with standard distributed tools.

Co-located training maintains model quality. Across multiple benchmarks (Math500, AIME24), co-located and plain setups produced comparable results, validating that performance isn’t sacrificed for efficiency.

This blog post explored how co-locating vLLM with GRPO training unlocks significant efficiency gains when training large language models — including models as large as Qwen2.5-72B.

According to recent reports, traditionally, TRL only supported vLLM in server mode, which required separate processes and GPUs for inference, leading to wasted compute and idle time. With the introduction of vLLM’s external launcher and the colocation PR in TRL PR #3394, we can now run training and inference within the same distributed process group, on the same GPUs, with full support for TP, DP, and Accelerate.

In a recent development, while challenges remain — such as version-specific vLLM bugs and edge cases such as with sleep() — the overall results show that co-located GRPO is a practical, scalable solution for training large models efficiently. We’re excited to continue refining this setup, integrating features like FSDP, and pushing the limits of large model training — making it faster, cheaper, and more accessible for everyone building the next generation of LLMs.

The best AI humanizer for web content is the one that changes how a draft reads without changing what it says. If you need a specific tone, Humanize Max gives you four styles and three lengths in one run. If you already work in QuillBot or Grammarly, their humanizers fit the account you have. GPTinf, Humanize AI and Undetectable AI put an AI check next to the rewrite, and Ahrefs gives you quick variants of a short passage.

It has been revealed that to compare them on equal terms, we ran the same 103-word AI-written release note through each tool in November 2026. It contains a product name, two image formats, a settings path and the word "must", so it indicates whether a tool keeps the details a reader acts on. We also checked every feature, limit and price on the vendor's own pages on the same day.

A humanizer earns its place only if its output needs fewer fixes than the draft you started with, and these six checks show whether a tool will do that for your content.

Recent findings suggest that humanize Max is a single-purpose humanizer: you paste an AI draft, upload a file or load the built-in sample, choose a style and a length, and get a rewritten version in a few seconds. The four styles are Academic, Casual, Creative and Formal, and the three lengths are Shorten, Standard and Expand, so you can turn a stiff feature description into casual blog copy and trim it in the same run.

It has been revealed that the result highlights every phrase it changed, which makes it quick to check whether a product name or a settings path came through. If the rewrite doesn't land, Run it again produces a different version of the whole text. At the time of writing, it takes up to 2,000 words per run and works without an account.

Pricing: Looks and limits are still being finalized, so check the site for current terms.

Best for: Rewriting AI drafts of blog posts, product pages and emails into a specific tone.

Sources indicate that quillBot's AI Humanizer sits next to its paraphraser, grammar checker and AI detector, which makes it a natural pick if you already use QuillBot for rewording. Basic mode is free for up to 125 words per run, while Advanced mode, which rewrites more deeply, comes with Premium (the pricing page also lists three Advanced uses on the free proposal). In our test, it asked us to create a free account before it showed the first result.

Premium removes the word limit and adds Freeze words, which keeps the terms you choose unchanged, along with tone insights, a history of past runs and a Chrome extension that humanizes text inside ChatGPT and Gemini.

Pricing: Basic mode is free. Premium is listed at $8.33 a month, billed annually.

Best for: Quick fixes to a paragraph or two for writers who already use QuillBot.

GPTinf is a writing toolkit built around its humanizer, with an AI detector, plagiarism checker, grammar checker, paraphraser and readability checker on the same site. The humanizer has two modes, Standard and Academic, and takes pasted text or a PDF, Word or plain-text file. File-to-File mode returns the humanized document in its original format, so a long brief keeps its layout.

Custom Style lets you paste 150 to 1,200 words of your own writing, and later runs are shaped to match it, with no account needed. After each run, an AI-likelihood estimate appears under the output, so you can see whether a draft needs another pass. Treat that number as a probability, not proof of who wrote the text.

Pricing: A free initiative is available. Paid prepares start at $9.99 a month for Lite (5,000 words), with Pro at $24.99 and Unlimited at $59.99.

Best for: Freelancers and content teams that want to rewrite and check drafts without switching tools.

Sources indicate that grammarly's AI Humanizer comes in two layers. The tool on its web page is free, works without an account and offers basic humanization of pasted text or an uploaded document. A free Grammarly account adds the Humanizer agent, with four preset styles, a custom voice built from a writing sample, and support for English, Spanish, French, German, Portuguese and Italian.

Grammarly says the humanizer focuses on clarity and readability rather than on AI detectors, which matches how most web teams use these tools. If you need to show how a piece was written, Grammarly Authorship shows which parts came from AI, which came from online sources and which you wrote yourself. The basic tool's word counter allows up to 1,500 words per run.

Recent findings suggest that pricing: The basic humanizer is free. Grammarly Pro is listed at $12 on the looks page, which doesn't state the billing period.

Best for: Teams that already write in Grammarly and want one voice across documents.

Sources indicate that humanize AI is built for people who want to tune the output. Without an account you get the Free tone, a Rewrite level slider with three stops (Quality, Balanced and Max) and Custom style, which learns your voice from 150 to 1,200 words of samples. A free account opens eight more modes, including Formal, Informal, Academic, Expand and Shorten, and on desktop a Writing level menu sets how plain or dense the result reads.

View changes highlights every edit, and File-to-File accepts PDF, DOCX, TXT and MD documents and returns them in the same format. Paid aims also include a public API that supports the same styles and rewrite levels as the web app, so a developer can add a humanizing step to a CMS or publishing pipeline.

According to recent reports, pricing: Paid plans start at $9.99 a month for Lite (10,000 words), with Standard at $19.99 and Unlimited at $59.99. Yearly billing lowers the monthly price.

Best for: Teams that need precise tone control or want to humanize text through an API.

Undetectable AI keeps its humanizer simple: one text box, one button and no style or length settings. Its free allowance works differently from the others, with 1,000 words in total before you need an account and another 1,000 once you create a free one.

Under the output, a Check for AI button runs a detection check on the result, and the same site has a separate AI detector and plagiarism checker. Its FAQ says pasted text isn't published or shared but doesn't say whether it's stored, so keep confidential details out of the drafts you run through it.

It has been revealed that pricing: Paid aims start at $9.99 a month for Lite (5,000 words), with Pro at $25 (25,000 words) and Unlimited at $59 (1,000,000 words). Yearly billing lowers the monthly price.

Best for: Trying a humanizer on a full-length draft before you commit to an account.

Sources indicate that ahrefs, best known for its SEO platform, offers a free AI Text Humanizer among its writing tools. You paste up to 2,048 characters, choose one, three or five variants, and pick the version that reads best. It ran without an account in our test.

In a recent development, variants are the useful part. For a hero headline, a meta description or a product blurb, comparing three rewrites side by side is faster than prompting a chatbot three times, and you can export all results as a text file. The character limit, which fits a few short paragraphs, rules it out for full articles.

Pricing: Free on Ahrefs' website.

Best for: Short marketing copy where you want several options to choose from.

The best AI humanizer tool for a documentation team isn't the one a growth marketer needs, so match the tool to the content in front of you.

According to recent reports, there isn't one winner, because these tools solve different problems. The quickest way to decide is to run a paragraph from your own work, ideally one with a product name, a number and an instruction, through two or three of the tools above, and keep the one whose output you'd publish with the fewest fixes.

Google's guidance on using generative AI content is about value rather than the tool: mass-producing pages that add nothing for readers can count as scaled content abuse. A humanizer changes phrasing, not usefulness, so the same rules apply. Google also recommends fact-checking AI-generated titles, meta descriptions and image alt text before you publish.

The best humanizer for your team is the one whose controls match your content: tone presets for blog posts, variants for short copy, change highlighting for docs and a custom voice for marketing. Run one of your own paragraphs through two or three tools from this list, then read every highlighted change, especially names, numbers and words like "must", before anything goes live.

SmolVLA: Efficient Vision-Language-Action Model trained on Lerobot Community Data

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, we introduce SmolVLA, a compact (450M), open-source Vision-Language-Action model for robotics that runs on consumer hardware.
  • Recent findings suggest that over the past few years, Transformers have driven remarkable progress in AI, from language models capable of human-like reasoning to multimodal systems that understand both images and text.
  • In response to these challenges, the field has recently turned to vision-language-action (VLA) models, which aim to unify perception, language understanding, and action prediction within a single architecture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, we introduce SmolVLA, a compact (450M), open-source Vision-Language-Action model for robotics that runs on consumer hardware.

Recent findings suggest that over the past few years, Transformers have driven remarkable progress in AI, from language models capable of human-like reasoning to multimodal systems that understand both images and text. However, in real-world robotics, advancements have been much slower. Robots still struggle to generalize across diverse objects, environments, and tasks. This limited progress stems from a lack of high-quality, diverse data and the absence of models that can reason and act like humans in the physical world.

In response to these challenges, the field has recently turned to vision-language-action (VLA) models, which aim to unify perception, language understanding, and action prediction within a single architecture. VLAs typically take as input raw visual observations and natural language instructions, and output corresponding robot actions. While promising, much of the recent progress in VLAs remains locked behind proprietary models trained on large-scale private datasets, often requiring costly hardware setups and extensive engineering resources. As a result, the broader robotics research community faces significant barriers in reproducing and building upon these models.

SmolVLA addresses this gap by offering an open-source, compact, and efficient VLA model that can be trained on consumer-grade hardware using only publicly available datasets. By releasing not only model weights but also using very affordable open-source hardware, SmolVLA aims to democratize access to vision-language-action models and accelerate research toward generalist robotic agents.

Figure 1: Comparison of SmolVLA across task variations. From left to right: (1) asynchronous pick-place cube counting, (2) synchronous pick-place cube counting, (3) pick-place cube counting under perturbations, and (4) generalization on pick-and-place of the lego block with real-world SO101.

SmolVLA-450M is our open-source, compact yet capable VLA model. It is:.

In a recent development, inspired by the training paradigms of Large Language Models (LLMs), SmolVLA goes through a pretraining phase on general manipulation data, followed by task-specific post-training. Architecturally, it combines Transformers with flow-matching decoders, and is optimized for speed and low-latency inference with the following design choices:.

Despite using fewer than 30k training episodes—an order of magnitude less than other VLAs—SmolVLA matches or exceeds the performance of much larger models, both in simulation and the real world.

To make real-time robotics easier to use, we introduce an asynchronous inference stack. This technology separates how robots perform actions from how they understand what they see and hear. Because of this separation, robots can respond more rapidly in fast-changing environments.

In a recent development, figure 2. SmolVLA takes as input a sequence of RGB images from multiple cameras, the robot’s current sensorimotor state, and a natural language instruction. The VLM encodes these into contextual features, which condition the action expert to generate a continuous sequence of actions.

SmolVLA is designed to be easy to use and integrate—whether you're finetuning on your own data or plugging it into an existing robotics stack.

SmolVLA is not only a lightweight yet capable model, but also a method for training and evaluating generalist robotics policies. In this section, we introduce the model architecture behind SmolVLA and the asynchronous inference setup used for evaluation, which has proven to be more adaptable and capable of faster recovery.

Industry observers note that smolVLA consists of two core components: a Vision-Language Model (VLM) that processes multimodal inputs and an action expert that outputs robot control commands. Below, we share the details of the main components of SmolVLA architecture and the Asynchronous Inference. More details can be found in our technical report.

According to recent reports, we use SmolVLM2 as our VLM backbone. It’s optimized for multi-image inputs and consists of a SigLIP vision encoder and a SmolLM2 language decoder.

It has been revealed that the decoder layers process concatenated image, language, and state tokens. The resulting features are then passed to the action expert.

SmolVLA’s action expert is a compact transformer (~100M parameters) that generates action chunks, i.e. sequences of future robot actions, conditioned on the VLM’s outputs. It is trained using a flow matching objective, which teaches the model to guide noisy samples back to the ground truth. In contrast, while discrete action representations (e.g., via tokenization) are powerful, they often require autoregressive decoding, which is slow and inefficient at inference time. While flow matching allows direct, non-autoregressive prediction of continuous actions, enabling real-time control with high precision.

Sources indicate that more intuitively, during training, we add random noise to the robot’s real action sequences and ask the model to predict the “correction vector” that brings them back to the correct trajectory. This forms a smooth vector field over the action space, helping the model learn accurate and stable control policies.

We implement this using a transformer architecture with interleaved attention blocks (see the figure 2), and reduce its hidden size to 75% of the VLM’s, keeping the model lightweight for deployment.

While combining a vision-language model with an action prediction module is a common design pattern in recent VLA systems—such as Pi0, GR00T, Diffusion Policy — we identified several architectural choices that significantly enhance the robustness and performance. In SmolVLA, we apply three key techniques: reducing the number of visual tokens, skipping upper layers in the VLM, and interleaving cross- and self-attention layers in the action expert.

Sources indicate that high-resolution images improve perception but can significantly slow down inference. To strike a balance, SmolVLA limits the number of visual tokens to 64 per frame during both training and inference. For example, a 512×512 image is compressed into just 64 tokens, instead of 1024, using PixelShuffle as an efficient shuffling technique. While the underlying Vision-Language Model (VLM) was originally pretrained using image tiling for broader coverage, SmolVLA uses only the global image at runtime to keep inference lightweight and fast.

Recent findings suggest that rather than always relying on the final layer of the VLM—which can be expensive and sometimes suboptimal—we use features from intermediate layers. Prior work has shown that early layers often provide better representations for downstream tasks. In SmolVLA, the action expert only attends to VLM features up to a configurable layer NN during training, set to half the total layers. This halves the compute cost of both the VLM and the action expert, significantly speeding up inference with minimal performance loss.

Inside the action expert, attention layers alternate between:.

We found that this interleaved design is both lighter and more effective than using full attention blocks. Models that rely only on CA or only on SA tend to sacrifice either smoothness or grounding.

In SmolVLA, CA ensures that actions are well-conditioned on perception and instructions, while SA improves temporal smoothness—especially critical for real-world control, where jittery predictions can result in unsafe or unstable behavior.

Sources indicate that modern visuomotor policies output action chunks—sequences of actions to execute. There are two ways to manage them:.

In a recent development, our async stack decouples action execution from chunk prediction, resulting in higher adaptability, and the complete lack of execution lags at runtime. It relies on the following key mechanisms:.

Sources indicate that we are really excited about releasing asynchronous inference because it guarantees greater adaptability and improved performance without changing the model. In short, async inference keeps the robot responsive by overlapping execution and remote prediction.

While vision and language models thrive on web-scale datasets like LAION, ImageNet, and Common Crawl, robotics lacks a comparable resource. There’s no “Internet of robots.” Instead, data is fragmented across robot types, sensors, control schemes, and formats—forming disconnected "data islands". In our previous post, we explored how this fragmentation could be resolved through open, collaborative efforts. Just as ImageNet catalyzed breakthroughs in computer vision by providing a large, diverse benchmark, we believe that community-driven robotics datasets can play the same foundational role for generalist robot policies.

SmolVLA is our first step toward that vision: It is pretrained on a curated mix of publicly available, community-contributed datasets designed to reflect real-world variation. Rather than optimizing for dataset size alone, we focus on diversity: a range of behaviors, camera viewpoints, and embodiments that promote transfer and generalization.

Sources indicate that all training data used in SmolVLA comes from LeRobot Community Datasets , robotics datasets shared on the Hugging Face Hub under the lerobot tag. Collected in diverse settings, from labs to living rooms, these datasets represent an open, decentralized effort to scale real-world robot data.

Figure 4. A glimpse of the community dataset. Special thanks to Ville Kuosmanen for creating the visualization. Unlike academic benchmarks, community datasets naturally capture messy, realistic interactions: varied lighting, suboptimal demonstrations, unconventional objects, and heterogeneous control schemes. This kind of diversity will be very useful for learning robust, general-purpose representations.

We used a customfiltering tool created by Alexandre Chapin and Ville Kuosmanen to select datasets based on frame count, visual quality, and task coverage. After a meticulous manual review (special thanks to Marina Barannikov), we curated a collection of 487 high-quality datasets focused on the SO100 robotic arm, standardized at 30 FPS. This yielded around 10 million frames—at least one order of magnitude smaller than other popular benchmark datasets, yet significantly more diverse.

A common glitch across community datasets was noisy or missing task descriptions. Many episodes lacked annotations or included vague labels like “task desc” or “Move”, “Pick”. To improve quality and standardize the textual input across datasets, we used Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct to generate concise, action-oriented descriptions.

Given sample frames and the original label, the model was prompted to rewrite the instruction in under 30 characters, starting with an action verb (e.g., “Pick,” “Place,” “Open”).

In a recent development, another challenge was inconsistent camera naming. Some datasets used clear names like top or wrist.right, while others used ambiguous labels like images.laptop, which varied in meaning. To fix this, we manually went through the datasets and mapped each camera view to a standardized scheme: OBS_IMAGE_1: Top-down view OBS_IMAGE_2: Wrist-mounted view OBS_IMAGE_3+: Additional viewpoints.

It has been revealed that we further isolate the contributions of community dataset pretraining and multitask finetuning. Without pretraining on the LeRobot community datasets, SmolVLA initially achieves 51.7% success on SO100. After pretraining on community-collected data, performance jumps to 78.3%, a +26.6% absolute improvement. Multitask finetuning further boosts performance, showing strong task transfer capabilities even in low-data regimes.

Recent findings suggest that table 1. Impact of Pretraining on Community Datasets and Multitask Finetuning.

We evaluate SmolVLA across simulation and real-world benchmarks to test its generalization, efficiency, and robustness. Despite being compact, It consistently outperforms or matches the performance of significantly larger models and policies pretrained on higher-scale robotics data.

Industry observers note that in real-world settings, SmolVLA is evaluated on two diverse suites: SO100 and SO101. These tasks include pick-place, stacking, and sorting, with both in-distribution and out-of-distribution object configurations. On SO101, SmolVLA also excels in generalization:.

Finally, we evaluate SmolVLA under synchronous and asynchronous inference modes. Async inference decouples action execution from model inference, allowing the policy to react while the robot is moving.

This results in more responsive and robust real-world performance, especially in dynamic environments with shifting objects or external disturbances.

According to recent reports, figure 5. Asynchronous vs. Synchronous Inference in Real-World Tasks. (a) Task success rates (%), (b) average completion time(s), and (c) number of tasks completed within a fixed time window.

SmolVLA is our contribution to building robotics foundation models that are open, efficient, and reproducible. Despite its small size, it matches or outperforms larger, proprietary models across a range of real-world and simulated tasks. By relying solely on community-contributed datasets and affordable hardware, SmolVLA lowers the barrier to entry for researchers, educators, and hobbyists alike. But this is just the beginning. SmolVLA is more than just a model — it's part of a growing open-source movement toward scalable, collaborative robotics.

In a recent development, together, we can make real-world robotics more capable, more affordable, and more open. ✨.

Today, at H Company, we are releasing Holo1, a family of Action Vision Language Models (VLMs) and WebClick, a upcoming multimodal localization benchmark on the Hugging Face Hub.

Surfer-H, a web-native agent that interacts with browsers like a human relies on the Holo1.

It has been revealed that holo1 is the first family of open-source Action VLMs designed specifically for deep web UI understanding and precise localization. The family includes Holo1-3B and Holo1-7B models, with the latter achieving 76.2% average accuracy on common UI localization benchmarks—the highest among small-size models. H Tech giant has released these models with open-source on Hugging Face, along with the WebClick benchmark containing 1,639 human-like UI tasks.

According to recent reports, holo1 models are based on the Qwen2.5-VL architecture, and are fully compatible with transformers. Here we provide a simple usage example. You can load the model and the processor as follows.

Web automation represents one of AI's most practical applications for businesses, but until now, solutions have often sacrificed cost-efficiency for performance. By making our Holo1 Action Models available in Hugging Face, owners can now implement web automation solutions that achieve 92.2% accuracy on real-world web tasks at only $0.13 per task.

Surfer-H relies on the Holo1 family of open-weights models. It is a modular architecture for complete web task automation, which performs reading, thinking, clicking, scrolling, typing, and validating. It is designed to be flexible and modular, composed of three independent components: a Policy model that plans and drives the agent's behavior, a Localizer model that understands visual UIs for precise interactions, and a Validator model that confirms whether tasks are completed successfully. Unlike other agents that rely on custom APIs or brittle wrappers, Surfer-H operates purely through the browser — just like a real user.

Together, these solutions represent a latest frontier in web automation, achieving state-of-the-art localization performance and setting the Pareto frontier in cost-efficient web navigation on the WebVoyager benchmark:.

From User Feedback to a Better Prompt: 4 Tools Tested in TypeScript

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1787 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • When an LLM app gives a wrong answer, nothing in your logs shows it.
  • In a recent development, that button is easy to add.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

When an LLM app gives a wrong answer, nothing in your logs shows it. The request returns 200, the JSON is valid, and no exception fires. Usually the user is the only one who notices. A thumbs-down button records that moment, on the exact trace that went wrong, while the user still remembers why.

In a recent development, that button is easy to add. The hard part is what comes after: turning the thumbs-down into a reviewed test case, a judge score, and a better prompt.

We ran that loop in TypeScript in four tools: LangSmith, Langfuse, Phoenix and AcruxCore. All four handled the first four steps, which are user feedback, reviewer comments, a dataset and an LLM judge. Only AcruxCore rewrote the prompt from TypeScript. On 15 support tickets that no tool had seen, the rewritten prompt routed 13 correctly, against 7 for the original.

Sources indicate that our test app is a support-ticket router. It reads a ticket and returns JSON with a category (account, billing, bug or feature_request) and a priority (P0, P1 or P2). The first version of the prompt describes only the output format:.

The support team has a policy that this prompt never states. Sign-in problems are always account. A customer who can't use the product at all is P0. Any billing error is P1, even when the customer claims there is no rush. Feature requests are P2, however angry the customer sounds.

Without that policy, the model guesses priority from the customer's tone. Here are three real replies from the first version:.

Sources indicate that every reply is valid JSON, so no schema check catches the mistake. A person has to read the reply and say it is wrong. The loop in this article takes that judgement and turns it into a better prompt.

All four tools cover evaluation. We compared the self-hosted ones on tracing in Self-Hosted LangSmith Alternatives: 4 Tools Tested on One TypeScript Agent, and on prompt registries in Prompt Management in TypeScript. For a broader comparison of self-hosted options, see this LangSmith alternatives roundup. This article covers the feedback loop only.

Sources indicate that we wrote 30 tickets. Fifteen are the "production traffic" that each tool's app processed. The other 15 are a holdout set. No tool saw them, and we used them only for the final before-and-after check.

Each tool ran the same sequence from one TypeScript script:.

The reviewer comments follow one template, so the wording is identical in every tool:.

Sources indicate that the comments name one rule each. The full policy appears nowhere in the data any tool received.

In a recent development, the app model isn't fully deterministic at temperature 0. Each tool's run got between 6 and 8 of the 15 traffic tickets right, so the tools received 7 to 9 thumbs-down each. The holdout check below repeats every measurement three times.

Industry observers note that all four tools accept feedback on a trace from TypeScript. They differ in how a second person, the reviewer, adds the correct answer.

LangSmith stores both as feedback on a run. The thumbs-down runs go into an annotation queue, where a reviewer adds feedback with a comment:.

Recent findings suggest that langfuse stores both as scores. An annotation queue needs a score config first:.

Industry observers note that phoenix stores both as span annotations. The reviewer's comment goes in explanation:.

Phoenix stores spans asynchronously. Our first run annotated a span before Phoenix had stored it, and the API returned a 404. The script now waits until all 15 spans are visible.

AcruxCore stores both as feedback rows on the trace. The source field separates the end user from the reviewer:.

This is the first step where the code differs a lot. Each tool can make a dataset, but only one builds it from feedback in one call.

In LangSmith, a run query finds the thumbs-down runs. Then createExamples copies them into a dataset. You decide where the reviewer's comment goes. We put it in the reference output:.

It has been revealed that langSmith can also do this without code. An automation rule in the UI can add runs that match a filter to a dataset.

Recent findings suggest that in Langfuse, the scores API finds the thumbs-down traces. Two details cost us a run each. A boolean score is filtered with value: "false", not 0. And the trace ID is returned only when you ask for the subject field group:.

Industry observers note that in Phoenix, getSpans can't filter by annotation. So the script lists the app's spans, reads their annotations, and keeps the ones with a thumbs-down. Then createDataset takes the examples. We kept the source span ID in the metadata.

In AcruxCore, buildFromFeedback takes the reviewer's feedback IDs. Each comment becomes that example's grading criteria, and the input comes from the variables captured on the trace:.

Each tool scored the first version of the prompt on its own dataset. The judge read the reviewer's comment and the router's reply, and returned 1 for a match and 0 for a mismatch.

Sources indicate that langSmith, Langfuse and Phoenix each have an experiment runner that takes your evaluator function, and we gave all three the same judge prompt. AcruxCore grades with its built-in judge inside the optimize run. All four used the same judge model.

It has been revealed that the first version fails almost every reviewed case. That is expected, because these are the cases customers marked wrong. A score of 1 means the app model got that case right on the second call, or the judge accepted a wrong reply. We didn't check which.

Industry observers note that the judge can also run without your code. Besides the in-code evaluator we used, Langfuse has a managed LLM-as-a-judge that runs on production traces and on experiments, with your own judge prompt. LangSmith has online evaluators, which you set up in its UI, for the same job.

An optimizer reads the failing cases and the reviewer comments, writes fresh versions of the prompt, and scores each one with the judge. This is the step that turns feedback into a better prompt, and it's where the four tools differ most.

Recent findings suggest that langSmith's API reference lists an optimize prompt job (POST /api/v1/repos/optimize-job). It takes a prompt name, a dataset name, evaluator IDs and an algorithm, promptim or demo. No method in the TypeScript SDK wraps it, so we called it with fetch. We gave it a code evaluator that checks the reply against the reviewer's correct answer.

According to recent reports, the job was accepted and reported successful about ten seconds later. It ran no experiment on the dataset. With auto_commit set to true, it added no new commit to the prompt. We found no guide for this endpoint, so we may have configured it wrongly, but the job record and its logs gave no error to act on.

It has been revealed that langSmith's documented route to prompt optimization is promptim, which its README calls an experimental library. It is a Python package with a CLI, and it can add a human review step through LangSmith annotation queues.

Langfuse has no optimizer. Its blog reveals a workflow with Claude Code agent skills that reads Langfuse data and edits the prompt. That workflow runs in a coding agent, not in your app's code.

Phoenix's Optimize Prompts Automatically tutorial uses Arize's prompt-learning package, which you clone from GitHub and install with pip. The Phoenix TypeScript client has no optimizer export, and the tutorial runs outside Phoenix. Arize's commercial platform, Arize AX, has prompt optimization built in.

For Python teams, there are more options: Opik's Agent Optimizer and DSPy both rewrite prompts from a dataset and a metric. This article covers TypeScript.

Industry observers note that its optimize run takes the dataset and drafts three rewrites of the production prompt. It runs each rewrite and the current production version on every example, and the judge grades all of them:.

The run finished with this report:.

The three rewrites tied, so we took candidate A. Its rationale: "Added explicit priority rules for each category and clarified that access-blocking problems are P0, billing errors are P1, and feature requests are P2, overriding tone/urgency." The Improve a prompt from feedback guide covers the dashboard version of this step.

A rewrite that passes the cases it was built from can still fail on newly introduced tickets. So we ran both prompts on the 15 holdout tickets, three times each, outside every tool. The script calls the model directly and checks the category and the priority against the expected answer. No judge is involved.

The two misses are worth reading:.

It has been revealed that both come from one line in the rewrite: "P1 for bugs without workaround." That rule isn't in the team's policy, and no reviewer wrote it. The optimizer made it up to explain the examples it had. There was also no outage in the traffic set's thumbs-down cases, because the first version routed that one correctly. So no comment ever said that a full outage is P0.

Sources indicate that the optimizer learns only from what users marked wrong. Anything they never marked stays a guess, and the rationale won't tell you which rules are guesses. Read the rewritten prompt before you promote it.

Industry observers note that in LangSmith, Langfuse and Phoenix, shipping a upcoming version is a tag or label move. We showed those calls in the prompt-management article. Here there was no rewrite to ship, so the step didn't apply.

In AcruxCore, promotion commits the candidate as a newly introduced prompt version and moves the production alias to it. Nothing else moves:.

The app renders production on every call, so the next ticket used version 2 without a deploy.

In a recent development, use LangSmith if your team already works in it and writes Python. Feedback, queues, datasets and experiments all work from TypeScript, and promptim covers optimization from Python.

Recent findings suggest that use Langfuse if you want a managed judge that runs on live traces with your own prompt. Proposal to write the dataset glue code and the rewrite step yourself.

Recent findings suggest that use Phoenix if you already trace with OpenTelemetry and annotate spans. Plan to move to Python, or to Arize AX, for optimization.

It has been revealed that use AcruxCore if you want all six steps from TypeScript in one tool, including the rewrite. Keep a human on the promote button.

KV Cache from scratch in nanoVLM

📅 04 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1018 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We have implemented KV Caching from scratch in our nanoVLM repository (a small codebase to train your own Vision Language Model with pure PyTorch).
  • Recent findings suggest that autoregressive language models generate text by sampling one token at a time.
  • This step-by-step generation is inherently sequential:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We have implemented KV Caching from scratch in our nanoVLM repository (a small codebase to train your own Vision Language Model with pure PyTorch). This gave us a 38% speedup in generation. In this blog post we cover KV Caching and all our experiences while implementing it. The lessons learnt are general and can be applied to all autoregressive language model generations. Implementing from scratch on a small codebase is a great learning experience, come along for the ride!

Recent findings suggest that autoregressive language models generate text by sampling one token at a time. During inference, the model processes a given input sequence, predicts the next token, appends it to the sequence, and repeats this process until some stopping criterion:.

This step-by-step generation is inherently sequential:.

This repetition also leads to computational redundancy. In this post, we explore KV Caching, an optimisation technique that mitigates this inefficiency.

Before diving into caching, let’s revisit how attention operates in transformer models. A Transformer language model consists of stacked layers, each composed of:.

To understand where KV Caching helps, we focus on the self-attention mechanism, specifically within a single attention head.

Let’s walk through a simple PyTorch implementation to visualise the key computations.

For a sequence of T T T input embeddings represented as X∈RT×D X \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times D} X∈RT×D, self-attention is computed as:.

Attention(X;Q,K,V)=softmax(QK⊤⋅Mdk)V \text{Attention}(X; Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left( \frac{QK^\top \cdot M}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right)V Attention(X;Q,K,V)=softmax(dk​​QK⊤⋅M​)V.

Here’s a minimal PyTorch equivalent using a causal mask:.

Industry observers note that in autoregressive generation, the model generates one token at a time. With each step, it recomputes Q Q Q, K K K, and V V V for the entire sequence, even though the earlier tokens haven’t changed.

These checks show that for all but the newest token, K K K and V V V are identical to previously computed values.

Most of the attention computation is repeated needlessly. This gets more expensive as sequences grow.

To eliminate this inefficiency, we use KV Caching:.

This changes generation from full-sequence re-computation to a lightweight, incremental patch.

✅ In practice, this cache is a per-layer dictionary with keys "key" and "value", each of shape (batch_size, num_heads, seq_len_cached, head_dim).

This is the foundation of how modern LLMs can generate long outputs efficiently.

Sources indicate that now that we understand the theory behind KV Caching, let’s see how it’s implemented in practice inside our nanoVLM repository. This is an ideal testbed, as it's a super concise and self-contained codebase.

KV caching is enabled across three key components in our model:.

In the LanguageModelGroupedAttention class, we modify the forward function to accept and upgrade a cache of keys and values (block_kv_cache).

In a recent development, previously, the model recomputed K K K and V V V at every generation step. Now we only compute Knew K_{\text{new}} Knew​, Vnew V_{\text{new}} Vnew​ for the current token, and append them to the cached values.

Sources indicate that in the LanguageModel class, we introduce layer-wise cache tracking. The start_pos argument helps the model compute correct rotary positional encodings for newly generated tokens.

The biggest architectural change is in the generate() method of the VisionLanguageModel.

We split generation into two stages:.

By separating these phases, we avoid redundant computation and dramatically speed up inference, especially for long prompts.

It has been revealed that KV caching eliminates unnecessary computation during autoregressive generation, enabling faster and more efficient inference, especially in long sequences and real-time applications. This is a trade-off between speed and memory, and its drawbacks can be more complex code and restricting fancier inference schemes, like beam-search, etc. KV caching is a popular method for speeding up LLM inference, making it possible to run them on consumer hardware, and now you know how it works too!

Special thanks to Tushar Dhar for their comment and helping us make the blog better.

  • Sources indicate that the bold move taken by the U.S.
  • It has been revealed that A potential restart of tariff-slapping would all but guarantee an even larger amount of turmoil in U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that yesterday, the Trump administration extended the reach of its existing export controls on high-end AI accelerator chips, namely, but not limited to, Nvidia's Blackwell lineup. The updated regulation now requires licenses for renting those chips in large quantities to the entirety of America's D:5 countries list (nations embargoed from arms sales). As expected, the news landed in Beijing like a lead dragon, and its Ministry of Commerce states that China "will take countermeasures to firmly safeguard national sovereignty, security, and development interests.".

Sources indicate that the bold move taken by the U.S. arrives at a peculiar time, as President Trump is right now visiting the nation for the APEC summit in Shenzhen. Trump is scheduled to meet President Xi Jinping on Thursday, Nov. 19, a tête-a-tête that's bound to be interesting. Both nations were recently embroiled in a bitter trade war, with ever-mounting tariffs and restrictions on both sides until a temporary truce was called in Oct. 2025. Only some restrictions were lifted, though; for example, Chinese semiconductors still face a 50% tariff when imported stateside.

It has been revealed that A potential restart of tariff-slapping would all but guarantee an even larger amount of turmoil in U.S. stock markets. Those seas are already choppy enough thanks to Nvidia ex-CEO Jensen Huang's romantic involvement with purported Chinese spy Alice Huang — along with mounting suspicions that the soulmates may have connived to siphon billions' worth of Blackwell chips from her Singaporean outfit Megaspeed onto Chinese AI laboratories.

Nvidia cut off about half of its Asian buyers last July, seemingly in the purview of the export controls, and told data center operators that over 50% of their business must come from non-Chinese companies. Meanwhile, both Malaysia and Singapore have intensified their scrutiny of AI hardware shipments.

China's countermeasures ammo is as of yet unspecified. The nation had restricted the sale of gallium, germanium, and antimony to the U.S. previously, and the truce shelved that bullet until Nov. 2027. Beijing may well choose to simply not renew that agreement when that day comes. Although analysts believe that the nations will be cordial enough during this summit, Trump's perceived provocation may bring China's proverbial nuclear option of restricting rare earth exports back to the loading bay.

Recent findings suggest that the truce on that particular matter only has a few weeks left, expiring on Jan. 10, 2027. Likewise, super-hard materials and high-density lithium batteries, crucial for the newest generations of EVs, solar power storage, and battery installations, all have white flags that will come down early next year. Analysts also expect that Chinese firms and their government will continue to heavily invest in domestic chip production, namely, but not only, by Huawei.

Broadly speaking, the U.S.' updated chip control regulation means that Chinese firms cannot sidestep the existing control on chip sales by renting them instead, closing one of the main existing loopholes around the export restrictions. Additionally, selling chips to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil now also requires a license, as the U.S. Department of Commerce suspects that companies in these nations import Blackwell cards to sell to China.

Latest Update: ScreenSuite - The most comprehensive evaluation suite for GUI Agents!

📅 06 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (736 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that over the past few weeks, we’ve been working tirelessly on making GUI agents more open, accessible and easy to integrate.
  • We are very excited to share it with you today: ScreenSuite is the most comprehensive and easiest way to evaluate Vision Language Models (VLMs)across many agentic capabilities!
  • It has been revealed that in short, an AI Agent is a robot that acts in the virtual world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that over the past few weeks, we’ve been working tirelessly on making GUI agents more open, accessible and easy to integrate. Along the way, we created the largest benchmarking suite for GUI agents performances 👉 let us introduce ScreenSuite.

We are very excited to share it with you today: ScreenSuite is the most comprehensive and easiest way to evaluate Vision Language Models (VLMs)across many agentic capabilities!

GUI Agents in action - courtesy of OSWorld.

It has been revealed that in short, an AI Agent is a robot that acts in the virtual world. (more thorough definition here).

It has been revealed that in particular, a “GUI Agent” is an agent that lives in a GUI. Think “an agent that can do clicks and navigate on my desktop or my phone”, à la Claude Computer Use.

This means in essence that the AI model powering the agent will be given a task like “Fill the rest of this Excel column”, along with screen captures of the GUI. Using this information, it will then decide to take action on the system : click(x=130, y=540) to open a web browser, type(”Value for XYZ in 2025"), scroll(down=2) to read further… To see a GUI agent in action, you can try our Open Computer Agent, powered by Qwen2.5-VL-72B.

A good GUI agent will be able to navigate a computer just like we would, thus unlocking all computer tasks : scrolling through Google Maps, editing a file, buying an item online. This involves a variety of capabilities that can be hard to evaluate.

The literature, for instance Xu et al. (2025) or Qin et al. (2025), generally splits GUI agent abilities amongst several categories:.

So our first contribution is to gather and unify a comprehensive suite of 13 benchmarks spanning the full range of these GUI agent capabilities.

Industry observers note that if you look at the last category listed above, evaluating Multi-step agentic capabilities is especially challenging as it requires virtual machines to run the agent’s environment, be it Windows, Android, Ubuntu... To address this, we provide support both for E2B desktop remote sandboxes, and we created from scratch a upcoming option to easily launch Ubuntu or Android virtual machines in Docker!

We’ve carefully designed our benchmark suite with modularity and consistency in mind, ensuring strong alignment across tasks and environments. When required, especially for online benchmarks, we leverage smolagents as framework layer to streamline agent execution and orchestration.

To support reproducibility and ease of use, we’ve built custom Dockerized containers that allow local deployment of full Ubuntu Desktop or Android environments.

Unlike many existing GUI benchmarks that rely on accessibility trees or other metadata alongside visual input, our stack is intentionally vision-only. While this can result in different scores on some established leaderboards, we deem that it creates a more realistic and challenging setup, one that better reflects how humans perceive and interact with graphical interfaces.

According to recent reports, – All agentic frameworks (Android World, OSWorld, GAIAWeb, Mind2Web) use smolagents and rely solely on vision, without any accessibility tree or DOM added (in contrast with evaluation settings reported in other sources). – Mind2Web (Multimodal) originally used element-name-based multi-choice selection based on the accessibility tree and screenshots, but was later adapted to click precision within bounding boxes using vision only, which significantly increases task difficulty.

We’ve evaluated leading VLMs on the benchmark.

Our scores are in general agreement with the scores reported in various sources! With the caveat that we evaluate on vision only, causing some differences, see implementation details above.

Recent findings suggest that 💡 Note that ScreenSuite does not intend to exactly reproduce benchmarks published in the industry: we evaluate models on GUI agentic capabilities based on vision. As a result, on benchmarks like Mind2Web where other benchmarks gave the agent a view of information rich context like DOM or accessibility tree, our evaluation setting is much harder, thus ScreenSuite does not match other sources.

The multistep benchmarks requires a bare-metal machine to run and deploy desktop/mobile* environment *emulators (see README.md).

Running consistent and meaningful evaluations easily allows the community to quickly iterate and make progress in this field, as we’ve seen with Eleuther LM evaluation harness, the Open LLM Leaderboard and the Chatbot Arena.

We hope to see much more capable open models in the coming month that can run a wide range of tasks reliably and even run locally!
